title: Indian Freedom Fighter Bhagat Singh Series in Development at Collective Studios’ Historyverse (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
A new original series exploring the life of Indian freedom fighter Bhagat Singh is in development at Collective Studios’ Historyverse. 

	The projec
body:
A new original series exploring the life of Indian freedom fighter Bhagat Singh is in development at Collective Studios’ Historyverse. 

	The project is being made in association with Hathiramani Commercial Ventures and co-produced with investor and entrepreneur Manish Hathiramani, who marks his producing debut with the show.

	The series is designed to move past the familiar episodes of Singh’s story and instead examine the man beneath the myth – his childhood, intellectual development and the social and political forces that shaped his convictions in early 20th-century India. Rather than revisiting the widely known chapters of Singh’s life, the show will track how his ideas evolved across the different stages of his journey, culminating in the revolutionary figure whose legacy continues to endure.
	

	Sudeep Lahiri, head of channels and distribution at Collective Media Network, said: “There are some figures in our history whose stories we think we know completely. Bhagat Singh is one of them. But behind the icon was a young man whose ideas, influences and experiences shaped the person he would become. That is the story we are interested in exploring. Having Manish come on board as a co-producer makes this collaboration particularly exciting, because we share a strong belief in finding new perspectives within stories that have already been told many times and bringing them to audiences with scale and ambition.”


	“Bhagat Singh is a figure whose life has always fascinated me, but what interests me most is the person before the legend,” Hathiramani added. “We know the revolutionary, the freedom fighter and the icon; this series gives us an opportunity to understand the many facets of Bhagat Singh’s life and the journey that shaped him. I am delighted to be producing this project with Historyverse and to bring a fresh perspective on his life and legacy to audiences.”
	

	Title, cast and additional details are to be confirmed. Singh has been the subject of at least five Indian features, among them “Shaheed” (1965), “Shaheed-E-Azam” (2002), “23rd March 1931: Shaheed” (2002), “The Legend of Bhagat Singh” (2002) and “Rang De Basanti” (2006). The Bhagat Singh project joins a Historyverse slate that already encompasses titles drawn from Indian mythology and history, including projects centered on Shivaji and Swami Samarth.

title: ‘The Wrong Girls’ Review: Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat Are a Good Time in Dylan Meyer’s Shaggy Stoner Comedy
description: Debut writer-director Dylan Meyer practically achieves liftoff with her absurdist stoner comedy “The Wrong Girls,” starring Kristen Stewart and Alia
body:
Debut writer-director Dylan Meyer practically achieves liftoff with her absurdist stoner comedy “The Wrong Girls,” starring Kristen Stewart and Alia Shawkat. If Method Man and Red Man once posited “How High” with their 2001 comedy, Meyer counters with a pair of pals who achieve psychic powers through experimental psychedelics. And while Dave Chappelle was “Half Baked” in 1998, put a fork in Frankie (Stewart) and Molly (Shawkat), because they’re fully done. The burnout duo, who live in an LA apartment dubbed Casa de Chill Zone, put Cheech and Chong to shame with their reefer madness. 
	

	Meyer blends together almost a few too many familiar strains for the plot of “The Wrong Girls,” which takes a minute to gain coherence before almost immediately losing it again. In this crazy California yarn, Frankie and Molly have to come up with rent money by the next day, as in F. Gary Gray’s 1995 LA stoner classic “Friday” (as well as last year’s “One of Them Days”), a quest that sends them on an odyssey fit for “Harold and Kumar Go to White Castle.” Meanwhile, a mistaken identity twist has a mercenary nicknamed Not Metal Head Dave (LaKeith Stanfield) and a team of Danish scientists and security contractors hot on their heels. Squid brains, talking cats and telepathy, oh my! 


	It may be loosey-goosey, but Meyer’s film is far from a bad trip. The ensemble cast is especially charming, and the good humor oozing out of the entire project means it’s hard to avoid a contact high. Stewart and Shawkat have a fun and amiable vibe together, even if their characters aren’t immediately in focus. Frankie is a Stanford engineering student who failed out of college and now works as a “Kwik Things” delivery driver. Codependent bestie Molly is a weed-inspired aspiring chef whose utterly reasonable boyfriend Josh (Zack Fox) would really love for her to get her life together and move in with him. 
	

	Frankie, on the other hand, discovers that her latest beau Mike Z. (Morgan Krantz) has replaced her with a straitlaced doppelgänger upgrade, Frances (Stewart in glasses). At a Mannequin Pussy show, she confronts the pair, then runs into the aforementioned Not Metal Head Dave, who passes her a secretive briefcase, thinking that Frankie is high-level researcher Frances. 

	Which is how Frankie and Molly find themselves in possession of some seriously heady psychedelics derived from deep sea squid testes. They make themselves unwitting test subjects for the stuff before trying to sell the drugs at a Stanford alumni event hosted by Martin (Tony Hale), and suddenly find themselves highly valuable assets for the drug researchers, including Dr. Olsen (Kate McKinnon), when it’s discovered they’ve gained telepathic powers during their trip.

	McKinnon is a comedic MVP as always, and Stanfield proves himself again to be a Swiss Army knife as a performer, ably fitting into any genre, role or ensemble cast, and demonstrating both comic chemistry with McKinnon and sexual chemistry with Stewart (one-sided on her part). Seth Rogen and Kumail Nanjiani voice Frankie and Molly’s cats to great effect. A Geena Davis cameo reminds us of another great film about female friendship, “Thelma & Louise,” though this one has a happier ending. 

	Cinematographer Todd Banhazl achieves the ‘90s retro druggie look with a brightly saturated palette, hazy filtered light, Dutch angles and wide lenses, while rocker-turned-composer Ty Segall lays down some nasty psych-surf rock guitar licks on the score — though some of the twangy flourishes get a touch repetitive.

	“The Wrong Girls” feels heavy on inside humor, much of it LA-centric — jokes about freeways, anyone? But Meyer is generous enough to want to bring the audience in on it, and she does make tangible her references. Those not in SoCal might not quite get the depths of the bit about Frankie and Molly mourning a restaurant called “Souper Starz Buffet” (R.I.P. Souplantation), but Meyer makes their tearful goodbye, and final feast, palpably emotional and fun to watch. 

	It all feels like a cult hit in a good way: the kind of movie you’d watch over and over on Comedy Central or on DVD because it’s just so silly, a little rough around the edges, but highly specific. It seems like that’s exactly what Meyer was going for too, so if that’s your thing, light it up and pass that Dutch.

title: Ritchie Blackmore Performs With Deep Purple for First Time Since Acrimonious Split in Early ’90s, After Warning Fans: ‘I Have Not Played Rock Music in 25 Years’
description: Most Deep Purple fans had long since given up any hope of seeing the band ever share a stage with founding guitarist Ritchie Blackmore again, due to
body:
Most Deep Purple fans had long since given up any hope of seeing the band ever share a stage with founding guitarist Ritchie Blackmore again, due to a well-know, decades-long estrangement. But that’s exactly what took place near the end of the group’s show Wednesday night at Jones Beach in New York, as hatchets were buried and Blackmore rejoined his old mates for a rendition of the group’s most famous song, “Smoke on the Water.”

	“It’s gonna be interesting,” Blackmore said in a podcast appearance the night before the show, in which the 81-year-old guitar legend leaked news of his imminent appearance. “i have not played rock music in 25 years.”
	

	At the conclusion of “Smoke in the Water” Wednesday, singer Ian Gillan showered praise on his ex-bandmate before he left the stage. “A couple of days ago I got a message from a local lad… saying ‘I only live around the corner, do you mind if I come and jam with you?’ It was an absolute pleasure to have back on stage the founding member, the great legend,”the immortal Ritchie Blackmore. Thanks, Ritchie. i have to say, it was a great pleasure. I’ll see you in the bar.”




	Probably few in the audience were taken by complete surprise by Blackmore’s cameo, since the previous night, the guitarist had spilled some of the beans in a livestream conversation with his wife, singer Candice Night, the evening before the Jones Beach gig. Blackmore said on Tuesday’s live podcast that he was revealing the secret in advance because he wanted fans who had waited for this moment for decades to at least have a shot at making it to New York in time for Wednesday’s show.
	

	Blackmore, who co-founded Deep Purple in 1968, had a fallout with other members in 1993 that resulted in him leaving the lineup in 1993 for the second and last time. The fallout was bad enough that Blackmore did not show up at the band’s Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction in 2016, after being told that the currently touring lineup — which still includes three original or near-original members in Gillan, drummer Ian Paice and bassist Roger Glover — would not reunite with him under any circumstances, even for a short, one-off performance at the ceremony.

	So hell seemed to have frozen over when Gillan recently sent a message gingerly asking if he could come up on stage for one number at a tour date… and the band proved surprisingly agreeable to that notion, after so much water under the bridge.

	“it is a secret and i don’t want anybody to know, but I’m probably going to go up and do an encore with the band, Deep Purple,” Blackmore blurted about eight minutes into the livestream with his wife, singer Candice Night. “But you can’t tell anybody, and I know this will be kept a secret. won’t it?” he joked, even as the web lit up with the news quickly being spread among hard rock buffs.

	Blackmore explained the genesis of this unexpected reunion: “I sent my AI pigeon to Ian Gillan in Portugal, where he lives at the moment, and I said, ‘How would you feel if I got up just for an encore on one of the songs. Don’t want to intrude.’ And I said, ‘No pressure, just kind of old times’ sake.’ You know, I’m 81 now. So (Gillan) seemed to li0e the idea, put it to the band, got a thumbs up, and it looks like we might be doing that.”

	The guitarist admitted he was hardly in practice for a performance with Deep Purple, given the drift in his musical focus since 1993, as he moved on to gentler brand of folk-rock with Blackmore’s Night, the band fronted by his wife.

	“I changed my strings on my Strat, which i haven’t done in over 25 years,” he revealed. “It’s kind of frightening. I haven’t played rock in 25 years. I’ve been playing acoustic guitar for 25 years. And at first i was very uncomfortable playing (acoustic guitar), but i got used to it, and now I’m more used to playing the acoustic, more so than the electric.”

	He said he needed some medical assistance in being able to withstand “Smoke on the Water.”
	

	“I did have my injection in my lumbar area yesterday,” he explained on the podcast, of needing a steroid shot. “it’s a special injection i have that enables me to stand in one spot, because if I’m playing a Strat, i have a hard time… I have four herniated discs, if anybody wants them. And I had my injection yesterday of a steroid which helps me get through standing on stage. But I have kind of a stool there, just in case I start toppling over or something.”

	Of his reasons for giving fans 24 hours’ notice, he said he “wanted to warn the people living in Romania, so they could fly over… Not really. I just thought it might be an idea to let a few people know because I think a lot of people would like to see that.”


	His announcement of sitting in with the group concluded with the thoughts: “I hope people enjoy it.” And: “it will be good to see the old guys again.”


	Fans from afar turned to the web to look for footage of the show. Perrin Wolfson and Jimmy Kay of the Metal Voice podcast livestreame through the latter part of Deep Purple’s set, waiting for confirmation that it had gone down, and putting up photos and video that were shared with them from inside the show. “History has been made,” Wolfson and Kay crowed as they first got word “Smoke in the Water” was in progress with Blackmore aboard. “I feel like we just walked on the moon.”

title: ‘Far From the Trees’ Director Meritxell Colell on Turning Exile and Endangered Languages Into a ‘Body of Memory’
description:
In “Far From the Trees,” (“Lejos de los árboles”) Meritxell Colell asks viewers to listen before they try to understand.

	Premiering in Locarno’s i
body:
In “Far From the Trees,” (“Lejos de los árboles”) Meritxell Colell asks viewers to listen before they try to understand.

	Premiering in Locarno’s international competition, the Spain-Italy-Peru production from Allegra Films follows Adela, a 50-year-old Mexican sound artist who travels from the Peruvian jungle to the Andes recording endangered languages. Accompanied by a guide and translator, she is continuing the work of her grandfather, a Catalan Republican exiled in Mexico. But news of her grandmother’s possible death fractures the journey, drawing Adela into childhood memories, family silences and fantastical visions.
	

	For the director, the film began with an absence.


	“‘Lejos de los árboles’ came into being in 2020 following the death of a very close family member. At the time, I knew only that I wanted to address the inability to say goodbye—the inability to view a dead body and the emotions that entails—and to link this to sound,” Colell told Variety.

	She initially searched for displaced or migrant sound artists and encountered Angélica Castelló, a Mexico-born, Vienna-based composer whose grandfather had also gone into exile. 

	“The film emerged from her story and those initial impulses; years later, I realized it also connected deeply with my own life – specifically, with the legacy of silence passed down by my grandparents,” Colell explained.

	Rather than reconstructing her own family history directly, she created Adela: a fictional figure whose identity is formed by migration, artistic vocation and the simple fact of being often elsewhere.
	

	“I was determined to center the film on the complexity of hybrid identities shaped by exile and migration –identities where the status of ‘foreigner’ becomes the self – and on the burden of that inheritance,” she said.

	The geographical distance was crucial. Adela follows her grandfather’s footsteps while transforming his political and anthropological work into art, weaving a sound map from languages at risk of disappearing. The connection between Indigenous languages in Peru and Catalan exile was not part of the earliest drafts, but became the idea that brought the film into focus.



	

	



	“Once the idea of vulnerable languages came up, everything fell into place,” said Colell. “It became clear that her work was carrying on her grandfather’s legacy, adding a new dimension to his figure.”

	The grandfather became an activist-anthropologist dedicated to recovering native languages in Mexico, a calling linked to his flight from a Catalonia where Franco’s regime suppressed languages other than Castillian Spanish.

	“In a way, the film is an ode to the beauty of languages, to their collective value, and to multilingualism as a viable social reality,” Colell says. “Language is a form of thought, a way of seeing and inhabiting the world. We don’t necessarily have to understand every form; we simply need to listen to them, however we can.”

	That principle shapes the film itself. We hear the birds, wind, voices, music, the whirr of a grandmother’s sewing machine and a thud against a trunk of a tree.

	“Sound is essential in cinema – not only on narrative and contextual levels but also on perceptual and emotional ones,” observed Colell. “That is why I was so eager to make a film featuring a sound artist as the protagonist.”

	The film’s Super 16mm passages, which inhabit memories, visions and reveries, were shot without synchronized sound. The voices of Adela’s grandparents and Paula were recorded separately, leaving Castelló free to build what Colell calls “a sonic tapestry woven from a multitude of sounds.”

	Castelló’s presence reshaped the film over years of residencies, meetings and debate. The director was determined, however, that Adela would firmly be fictional rather than becoming a portrait of the performer.
	

	“It was a way to lighten the role, turn it into a game, and distance it from reality,” she said. “It was crucial for me to portray a person in her fifties who had left her home country to pursue her passion– music – and to depict a type of woman rarely seen on screen.”

	“As time went on, my initial intuition upon meeting her was confirmed: She was the film.”

	Producer Mayca Sanz L-Higueras began assembling the project in 2021, initially seeking a European structure that could connect with Latin America through Ibermedia. Italy’s Exit Media joined first; Peru’s Animalita Cine later came on board, while RTVE helped complete the financing.

	“In Peru, the biggest challenge has been finding someone willing to commit to filming with a fiction crew – albeit a very small one – in a country completely unprepared for such a project, and with a story that required the commitment of non-professional actors whom the director had sought out, selected and worked with over time, following location scouting trips spanning three years,” said Sanz.

	The shoot unfolded in five blocks over more than a year, beginning in February 2024 and ending with Teresita Sánchez’s scenes in July 2025. Colell also became a mother during production.

	“At times, I worried that shooting in such fragmented stages might result in something of a Frankenstein’s monster; I’m used to filming in chronological order,” she says. “The surprise came when we started editing and saw that everything actually fit together perfectly.”

	For Allegra Films, Locarno’s selection validates a leap into a more ambitious international model. For Colell, it offers a setting suited to a film that resists tidy explanations.

	“I love open cinema– films that engage the viewer and connect them to their own lived experience. Cinema that pierces you and settles deep in your gut, beneath your skin, in your chest,” she says.

	She hopes younger viewers will leave the screening wanting to investigate the history of exile, or to ask their own relatives what was never said.

	“The film speaks to the need to listen, the importance of passing things on, and how we people act as both transmitters and receivers of memory,” said Colell. “And, in a sense, the film itself is a body of memory.”
	

	The collaboration between director and lead allows “Far From the Trees” to examine the cost of building a life elsewhere. Adela’s strained relationship with those tasked with caring for her grandmother, raises questions about who stays, who leaves and who inherits responsibility.

	“Distance is inherently complicated, yet it can also be liberating,” said Colell. “I wanted to explore this issue without judgment: to discuss the consequences of living far from family, how that shapes one’s identity, and how it affects those who take on caregiving duties.”

	She recalls Castelló telling her: “I am a permanent foreigner. My home – my refuge – is sound. Music.”

	“That statement encapsulates the film’s central quest,” Colell concludes. “I would love for the film itself to become that home, that refuge.”

schema.headline: ‘Far From the Trees’ Director Meritxell Colell on Turning Exile and Endangered Languages Into a ‘Body of Memory’

title: Hollywood’s Top-Grossing Films of 2025 Show Limited Progress Toward Inclusion, Study Says: ‘The Pace of Change Has Been Slow’
description: After nearly 20 years of tracking representation metrics, the latest report from Dr. Stacy L. Smith and the Annenberg Inclusion Initiative reveals t
body:
After nearly 20 years of tracking representation metrics, the latest report from Dr. Stacy L. Smith and the Annenberg Inclusion Initiative reveals that Hollywood’s film industry has not made lasting progress towards inclusion. 

	“While we’ve seen pockets of progress for women on screen, the pace of change has been slow. Year after year, many of the same patterns remain,” Dr. Smith said in a statement about the study. “Incremental improvement is important for achieving meaningful transformation, but after nearly 2 decades of research and advocacy from many groups, it is clear that the industry is content to wait for change to find them rather than pursuing solutions.”
	

	Smith’s statement accompanies the Annenberg Inclusion Initiative’s annual report, titled “Inequality in 1,900 Popular Films,” which examines representation and inclusion metrics for the 100 top-grossing films of 2025. The study evaluates representation on camera (based on gender, race/ethnicity, the LGBTQ+ community and people with disabilities) and behind the scenes (the gender and race/ethnicity of directors, writers, producers, composers and casting directors), adding to a dataset that began in 2007.


	Some key takeaways from the study include that, despite comprising just over 50% of the U.S. population, in 2025, just 33.6% of all speaking or named characters were women and girls. Remarkably, that figure hasn’t changed much in 19 years (29.9% in 2007). In terms of lead or co-lead roles, women and girls have seen progress (38 films in 2025 compared to 20 in 2007), but the figure dipped from the 19-year high of 55 lead/co-lead roles in 2024. Of those 38 films, 15 had a female lead/co-lead from an underrepresented racial or ethnic group, and 3 had a female lead/co-lead 45 years of age or older. Only 4 nonbinary speaking or named characters were coded across the sample. 
	

	LGBTQ+ representation on screen remained static from 2024, with 36 speaking or named characters (less than 1%) in 2025, but not one transgender character appeared in the sample. The percentage of characters with a disability also stayed relatively stagnant at 2.8% (121 characters). 

	When it came to representation behind the scenes, the study further contextualizes an earlier report that only 9 of the 111 directors who helmed 2025’s top-grossing films were women: Nisha Ganatra (“Freakier Friday”), Emma Tammi (“Five Nights at Freddy’s 2”), Domee Shi (“Elio”), Madeline Sharafian (“Elio”), Celine Song (“Materialists”), Jennifer Kaytin Robinson (“I Know What You Did Last Summer”), Maggie Kang (“KPop Demon Hunters”), Hikari (“Rental Family”) and previous best director Oscar winner Chloé Zhao (“Hamnet”). The percentage and number of women directors in 2025 has significantly decreased since 2024 (a record high 16 women), but was identical to 2008. Across all 19 years, just 7% of directors were women.

	Women writers and producers filled 16% and 24.4% of their respective roles in 2025, a figure that hasn’t markedly changed from 2007. The greatest change was observed for women composers, whose employment has surged since 2007, when there were no women composers working across the top 100 movies. In 2025, 10 women (8.5%) were credited with working as composers.

	In terms of racial and ethnic diversity, 41.5% of all speaking or named characters were from an underrepresented group, a figure that reaches proportional representation to the world’s population for just the fourth time in 19 years. Since 2007, the percentage of white characters fell by 19.1%; however, only the percentage of Asian characters has increased significantly (by 11.1%).  And there are still significant ways that groups were left out of storytelling: 30 movies did not have any Black characters, 46 were missing Hispanic/Latino characters, and 26 excluded Asian characters. 

	“Nineteen years of data show that change is possible, but they also show how fragile that progress can be,” said Dr. Smith. “This is not the first time this report has shown that meaningful gains are followed by a return to business as usual. At a moment when the industry is redefining its future, inclusion can be part of the solution, not a casualty of contraction. The question is no longer whether the industry can change. It’s whether it will.”
	

	For the full report, visit the Annenberg Inclusion Initiative website.

	[Pictured above (clockwise): “One of Them Days,” “KPop Demon Hunters,“ “Freakier Friday“ and “Hamnet“]

schema.headline: Hollywood’s Top-Grossing Films of 2025 Show Limited Progress Toward Inclusion, Study Says: ‘The Pace of Change Has Been Slow’

title: BTS’ V Reveals Right-Ear Hearing Loss Amid World Tour
description: BTS member V told fans in a Wednesday livestream that he is being treated for hearing loss affecting his right ear, which he said now functions at r
body:
BTS member V told fans in a Wednesday livestream that he is being treated for hearing loss affecting his right ear, which he said now functions at roughly a third of the level in his left. 

	He said he initially did not take the issue seriously, calling it “a matter of mental strength,” but is now taking medication and attending regular hospital appointments to manage it, according to BBC News.


	The disclosure landed midway through the band’s Arirang World Tour, which launched in South Korea in April and reunited all seven members for the first time in years following their individual stints in the military. Wednesday’s livestream came after the group wrapped tour dates in Baltimore, Maryland; upcoming stops include Los Angeles, Buenos Aires, Bangkok, Sydney and Hong Kong.
	

	V, whose real name is Kim Tae-hyung, said his hearing problems worsened during his military service, which he began in 2023 before being discharged in June 2025. South Korea requires nearly all able-bodied men to complete 18 months of service, a rule that applied to all seven BTS members, who began enlisting in 2022 at the height of the group’s global popularity.

	Jungkook, V’s fellow BTS member, also joined the livestream, describing a shin injury he has been managing throughout the tour. He said he is close to developing a stress fracture and will need to carefully manage the injury in order to keep performing.

	In July, BTS sent shockwaves through the music industry when they said they would not submit its music for consideration at the 69th Grammy Awards,  after the Recording Academy unveiled a new Best Asian Pop Music Performance category. In response, Grammy CEO Harvey Mason jr. said, “The Asian Pop category was created to celebrate the depth, diversity and extraordinary growth of pop artistry coming out of Asia. The spirit of this new category is to shine a dedicated spotlight on these important artists. More categories mean more artists’ work is recognized. It’s never to divide, but to expand who is recognized by our 15,000 Grammy voters.”

title: Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market Names Japan 2026 Focus Country for Producer Hub
description: The Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) has selected Japan as the 2026 Focus Country for its Producer Hub, a co-production networking platform tied
body:
The Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM) has selected Japan as the 2026 Focus Country for its Producer Hub, a co-production networking platform tied to the Busan International Film Festival (BIFF(.

	Japan will send 10 producers to Busan in October for project pitching, speed meetings and case-study sessions.

	Now in its third year, Producer Hub gives producers pursuing international co-productions a forum to trade information and build relationships. The initiative singles out one focus country annually, using the selection to showcase that market’s production landscape, incentive programs and slate of in-development projects.
	

	This year’s Japanese delegation will pitch active co-production projects, detail how the country’s production system operates and look for new partners across the region, according to ACFM.


	ACFM launched Producer Hub in 2024 as a dedicated space for producers to compare notes on financing, investment and local support schemes across different territories.

	Korea held the inaugural focus country slot in 2024, co-hosted by the Korean Film Council. Canada took the spot in 2025 alongside Telefilm Canada, an edition that drew 154 producers representing 25 countries. That exchange takes on added significance following an audiovisual co-production treaty Canada and the Korea signed in 2026, which organizers expect will deepen ties between the two countries. Producer Hub’s partner network has meanwhile grown from eight organizations in seven countries at launch to 13 organizations across 10 countries today.

	Producer Hub 2026 runs four days, from Oct. 10 to 13 – one day longer than the 2025 edition. The Japanese delegation will pitch in-development projects and detail the country’s production environment, while separate case-study sessions will examine past co-productions between Japan and other countries. Speed meetings and networking sessions round out the schedule.
	

	Organizers added the extra day to give participants more room to build on early conversations. Follow-up sessions are being arranged specifically with the Japanese producers so that discussions started during speed meetings can continue, moving past introductions into details on projects, production conditions and potential collaboration, according to ACFM.

	ACFM Director Ellen Y.D. Kim said, “Japan today is Asia’s most dynamic co-production partner. Building on its longstanding strength in independent and arthouse cinema, international collaboration is expanding on all fronts to encompass commercial films and series, backed by bold policies centered on grants and incentives,” adding, “Together with Japan, this year’s focus country, Producer Hub aims to serve as a platform offering producers across Asia tangible opportunities for collaboration.”

	Producer Hub plans to keep expanding its roster of partner organizations beyond the current 13 across 10 countries. Producers interested in international co-production can apply via the ACFM website, with the application window open through Aug. 31.

	ACFM runs in Busan each October alongside BIFF. The market’s 20th edition in 2025 was its largest yet, with registration reaching 1,222 companies and 3,024 professionals across 55 countries and total on-site attendance hitting 30,006. Its Sales Market logged 8,438 business meetings, with a transaction value estimated at $71.1 million.

	The 2026 Asian Contents & Film Market runs Oct. 10–13 at BEXCO’s Exhibition Center 2 in Busan, alongside the 31st Busan International Film Festival, set for Oct. 6–15.

	Japan was also the country of honor at this year’s Cannes Film Market.

schema.headline: Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market Names Japan 2026 Focus Country for Producer Hub

title: Andreas Dresen, Doris Dörrie Films to World Premiere  at Zurich Film Festival
description: The world premieres of two major German films, Andreas Dresen’s “Love, After All” and Doris Dörrie’s “How Can I Help?,” are among 11 titles to featu
body:
The world premieres of two major German films, Andreas Dresen’s “Love, After All” and Doris Dörrie’s “How Can I Help?,” are among 11 titles to feature in the Gala Premieres section of Zurich Film Festival.

	The selection also includes Oscar contenders “I Play Rocky” and “Josephine,” and Switzerland’s most anticipated film, “111 – Echoes From Halifax.”

	Christian Jungen, CEO of the festival, said the section is “dedicated to auteur cinema for a broader audience.”
	

	“We are particularly delighted that two major figures of German auteur cinema, Andreas Dresen and Doris Dörrie, have entrusted us with the world premieres of their new films,” Jungen said. “Their films are grounded in everyday life and, with a little wink, reflect on the state of our society.”


	He added, “We present films that will play an important role later in the award season, such as ‘I Play Rocky.’” The film tells the story behind the making of the cult classic starring Sylvester Stallone, which won the Academy Award for best picture in 1977.

	Jungen explained that, from a Swiss perspective, “111 – Echoes From Halifax” deserves special mention. “From multiple perspectives, the film sheds light on a major event that shook our nation: the crash of a Swissair aircraft near Halifax,” he said.

	The full program of the 22nd Zurich Film Festival, which runs Sept. 24 to Oct. 4, will be revealed on Sept. 9.

	I PLAY ROCKYEuropean PremiereBiographyU.S., 2026Director: Peter FarrellyCast: Anthony Ippolito, Matt Dillon, Stephan James, AnnaSophia Robb, PJ Byrne, Toby Kebbell, Tracy Letts, Jay DuplassUnknown actor Sylvester Stallone is writing a screenplay titled “Rocky” that a studio is desperate to acquire. But Stallone refuses to sell the rights – unless he gets to play the lead himself. Despite numerous setbacks and rejections, he remains determined to make his dream a reality: playing Rocky Balboa. The result is the ultimate underdog story behind the legendary underdog film.
	

	JOSEPHINEDramaU.S., 2026Director: Beth de AraújoCast: Channing Tatum, Gemma Chan, Mason Lily ReevesWhen 8-year-old Josephine witnesses a violent crime, her world is out of joint. She is trying to find a way to regain a sense of security. While her emphatic mother (Gemma Chan) wants to help her process what happened, her father (Channing Tatum) believes in preparing Josephine for the harsher realities of life but increasingly finds himself overwhelmed by the situation. With the suspense of a thriller, director Beth de Araújo tells a deeply empathetic family drama about fear and the limits of parental care. Channing Tatum gives one of his strongest performances in this year’s great Sundance Film Festival sensation.

	WICKERComedyU.S., 2025Director: Alex Huston Fischer, Eleanor WilsonCast: Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård, Peter Dinklage, Elizabeth Debicki, Marli Siu, Nabhaan RizwanAn audacious comedic fable about sex, marriage and the absurdities of social convention, “Wicker” tells the wholly original love story of an ostracized fisherwoman (Colman) who commissions a husband to be made by the local basketmaker (Dinklage). When her wicker husband (Skarsgård) proves more spectacular than she ever imagined, his soulful spirit and unique prowess awaken something inside her, setting off a wave of jealousy, fascination and upheaval that threatens the very fabric of village life.

	111 – ECHOES FROM HALIFAXInternational PremiereDramaSwitzerland, Canada, 2026Director: Mauro MuellerCast: Ursina Lardi, Kris Holden-Ried, Djebril Zonga, Fathia Youssouf, Natalie BrownOn Sept. 2, 1998, the crash of Swissair Flight 111 off Halifax changes the lives of many people forever: relatives struggle for certainty about their loved ones, helpers try to offer comfort, and the residents of the Canadian coast are confronted with the traces of tragedy. As time passes and questions remain unanswered, the film shows how grief connects, relationships change, and new perspectives emerge. Mauro Mueller’s film is a quiet, poignant drama about loss, memory and the power of human closeness.

	COMPANYMysteryCanada, U.S., UAE, 2026Director: Casey AffleckCast: Nick Nolte, Ben Mendelsohn, Adelaide Clemens, Scoot McNairy, Emily Alyn Lind, Caylee CowanOn a winter night in 1975, a mysterious woman named Evelyn arrives uninvited at a holiday gathering and tells the story of Tom, an aging hermit who rescues a stranded actress during a Colorado blizzard in 1953. To pass the night, the actress recounts an older tale of a farming couple who take in a troubled young drifter as a series of grisly murders spreads fear across the frontier. As the stories intertwine across generations, “Company” becomes a meditation on grief, vengeance, forgiveness and the quiet acts of compassion that can heal even the deepest wounds.
	

	POSSIBLE LOVEDramaSouth Korea, 2026Director: Lee Chang-dongCast: Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung, Cho Yeo-jeong“Possible Love” follows the intertwined relationship of two married couples facing different paths and hidden desires. Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon) lives quietly with her laid-off husband Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu) and their young son Cheol until a funeral brings them into the orbit of Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong), a documentary filmmaker chronicling laid-off workers, and her husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung) – a couple whose affluent lifestyle stands in sharp contrast to their own. When Mi-ok agrees to be filmed, she grows close to Ye-ji, and finds herself uneasily drawn to the unreadable Sang-woo. As their worlds collide, fractures begin to appear in their daily existence. Marking his first release in eight years, highly acclaimed director Lee Chang-dong (“Burning,” “Poetry,” “Secret Sunshine”) brings his signature nuance to “Possible Love,” capturing shifting emotions, conflicts, and contrasting outlooks that shape these relationships.

	LOVE, AFTER ALLWorld PremiereTragicomedyGermany, 2026Director: Andreas DresenCast: Dagmar Manzel, Joachim KrólLore (Dagmar Manzel) and Harry (Joachim Król) have been married for nearly 40 years and there is rarely a moment of silence between them. Old stories, missed chances and the uncertainties of retirement fuel heated discussions. Lore is afraid of growing old and bitter in the garden alongside Harry while he longs for stability and peace. There is only one thing they agree on: Their daughter Gloria has little luck in love. Now, she wants to get married for the third time – this time to a wealthy man who is almost the same age as Harry. A warm-hearted love story inspired by real life, drawing the audience in with its authentic characters and lots of humor.

	IT WILL HAPPEN TONIGHTRomanceItaly, France, Spain, 2026Director: Nanni MorettiCast: Louis Garrel, Jasmine Trinca, Hippolyte Girardot, Angela Finocchiaro, Melina Åkerman Kvie, Elena Lietti, Andrea Lattanzi, Antonio De Matteo, Nanni MorettiI’ll wait for you, for as long as you want me to. But will it ever happen?

	BURGUNDYDocumentaryFrance, 2026Director: Michael Dweck, Gregory KershawCast: Enzo Ferraroli, Céleste Kalis, Eric Goettelmann, Patrick Maniere, Guillaume Baroin, Bertrand DevillardBurgundy is one of the world’s most famous wine regions. Through the eyes of novices in hospitality and viticulture, the film offers a fascinating glimpse into its unique wine culture, where time-honored traditions live on in rituals centered on luxury and indulgence. Blending documentary and fictional elements, directors Michael Dweck and Gregory Kershaw pay homage to the remarkable and charming people whose zest for life shapes and preserves this unique region and its centuries-old culture.
	

	HOW CAN I HELP?World PremiereDrama/ComedyGermany, 2026Director: Doris DörrieCast: Angela Winkler, Laura Tonke, Josef Ellers, Via Jikeli, Eugene Boateng, Zoë BaierMrs. Winkler has a fall and becomes a nursing case. Her daughter, overwhelmed by her needs, hires a care robot. After some initial resistance, Mrs. Winkler grows quite fond of him. He takes perfect care of her and keeps her entertained – except that he is also supposed to kill her in case her condition deteriorates further…

	THE HAMMERWorld PremiereDocumentaryFrance, U.S., 2026Director: Simon WallonCast: Simon de Pury, Jeff Koons, Marina Abramović, Chloe Wise, Lou ZhenggangA documentary portrait of famed auctioneer Simon de Pury, whose career saw him leading auction houses such as Sotheby’s and Phillips, being the curator of major world collections, an artist, even a DJ, and always being an unavoidable personality “the Mick Jagger of auctions” takes us behind the curtain of the extravagant art market. Art fairs, collectors’ homes, artists’ studios, galas… The film is a welcoming and entertaining dive amongst the 1% and explores the complicated relationship between artists and commerce. Ultimately, it questions what it means to be an artist today. It was shot between New York, Tokyo, London, Cannes, Miami and Monaco.

title: Haugesund New Nordic Films Reveals Standout 36 Nordic Projects and 15 Fresh Pics Set to Woo 300 Industry Attendees
description: New Nordic Films, the industry confab and side-kick to the Norwegian International Film Festival in Haugesund, Norway, has revealed today the full l
body:
New Nordic Films, the industry confab and side-kick to the Norwegian International Film Festival in Haugesund, Norway, has revealed today the full list of anticipated Nordic features selected for its 32nd edition running Aug. 25-28.

	One of New Nordic Films’ hottest showcases, the Nordic Co-Production Market (NCPM) will platform 21 titles in development, picked among more than 120 submissions, a record level on par with 2025, according to head of industry Gyda Velvin Myklebust. The veteran industry honcho underscored the exceptional lineup from Norway — nine final picks from 30 submissions, including five debuts.On the watch list, available for sales, are two female helmers turning to horror with the backing from pedigreed producers.
	

	The supernatural horror “Vagina Dentata,” is the fiction debut of Oslo-based Nataša Urban, CPH:DOX winner and IDFA and MoMa selected with her 2022 doc “The Eclipse.” Teaming up with her is seasoned doc producer Ingvil Giske of Medieoperatørene, behind the Sundance winners “The Remarkable Life of Ibelin” and “The Painter and the Thief.”


	Set in 1349 Western Norway, the female empowering “The Virtuous” by Ina Grevstad is produced by Mer Film, behind “Sentimental Value” and “The Ugly Stepsister.”

	Another hot Norwegian female helmer — Jorunn Myklebust Syversen (“Disco,” “The Tree Feller)” will direct the social drama “Patience” for top Norwegian banner Paradox, while Haugesund-born Pål Jackman (“Detektor,” “The Storm in My Heart”) makes his comeback to feature film after a string of successful series (“A Sámi Wedding,” “State of Happiness”) with the family drama “Domesticated Animal.”
	

	Among other established Nordic names, Iceland’s Hilmar Oddsson (“Driving Mum” ) will pitch the drama about Alzheimer “At the End of the Road,” Finland’s AJ Annila (“The Eternal Road”) the period drama “The Touch of Light,” and Sweden’s Martina Haag the feelgood comedy “True Love.”As announced exclusively in Variety, four French projects looking for co-financing and distribution, mostly from the Nordics, will also be showcased at the Nordic Co-Production Market as part of the French Focus: “All the Softness in the World,” “Boutès,” ”Boderline” and “Temporary Lives.”

	A similar blend of genres, quality Nordic pics from seasoned and rising talent plays out in the 15 title Works in Progress, selected from 43 submissions. “It’s been easier this year to select high quality projects in post-production, perhaps because it’s harder to reach the market or harder to get international recognition,” reflected Myklebust.

	Animation Rules



	

					‘ViQueens’ marks the animation debut of director Harald Zwart.
									Courtesy of Zwart Arbeid
	



	The industry head pointed at animation as a genre strongly featured this year across the Nordic Co-Production Market and Works in Progress with three projects in each section.

	Headlining the slate in post is “ViQueens,” the animation debut of Norwegian/Dutch blockbuster habitué Harald Zwart (“The Karate Kid,” “The 12th Man”). Teased in Berlin and Annecy, the epic Viking tale produced by Veslemøy Ruud Zwart boasts a stellar English language voice cast including Ella Purnell, Rita Ora, Alan Carr and Anton Lesser. Sola Media handles sales.

	Another high-quality family animation pic: “Millie and the Secret of the Crocodile,” directed by the established Esben Toft Jacobsen (“The Great Bear,” “Beyond, “Beyond”) for Sweden’s Snowcloud, has secured world distribution with LevelK, while “Saajve,” the first ever Sámi animation project, will be looking for sales in Haugesund.



	

					Alba August and Gustav Lindh star in Charlotte Sieling‘s ‘The Closed Book’
									Courtesy of SF Studios
	



	Among commercially-oriented names, Denmark’s Christian E. Christiansen, Oscar-nominated for his short “At Night“ (2007), will pitch “Rawhood,” a sequel to his 2006 hit “Life Hits,” produced by Zentropa; Charlotte Sieling (“Margrete-Queen of the North,” “Borgen”) the adaptation of Jette A. Kaarsbøl’s historical novel “The Closed Book,” produced by SF Studios; and Jens Lien (“The Bothersome Man”) his much anticipated AI-driven “Joe’s Assignment,” produced by Einar Film (“Handling the Undead”).

	Fast-rising Swedish talent Fanny Ovesen whose “Live a Little,” repped by LevelK, was snatched for the U.S. by Breaking Glass Pictures last year in Haugesund, will unveil clips of her new coming-of-age pic “The Excursion,” produced in Norway by Maipo Film, and Daniel Sawka his autism spectrum disorder (ASD) romcom “Love and Other Disorders,” pitched in 2024 at the Nordic Co-Production Market.
	



	

					‘The Horsemen of the Apocalypse’ by Lene Berg
									Courtesy of Twentyone Pictures
	



	Myklebust also highlighted the Norwegian documentary “The Horsemen of the Apocalypse,” in which artist and filmmaker Lene Berg turns on the traumatic childhood memory of the year 1975, when her father, the famed filmmaker Arnljot Berg, was arrested in Paris, accused of the murder of his wife.

	New Nordic Films’ third pillar — the closed market screenings —  will showcase 18 titles among the most high-profile Nordic productions or co-productions, such as Cristian Mungiu’s Palme d’or winner and New Nordic Films opener “Fjord,” Norwegian International Film Festival opener “Beloved” by Erik Poppe and San Sebastian competition-bound “Growth of the Soil” by Hans Petter Moland.

	In total, nearly 300 professionals from 28 countries — of which 50-plus distributors, 20 sales agents and 20 festival programmers — have signed up for the Nordic industry event.

	On the panel front, New Nordic Films’ long-standing partnership with Europa Distribution will deliver practical case studies on “Sentimental Value” and “The Love That Remains” to illustrate The International Success of Nordic Cinema, while Morten Tyldum’s anticipated pic “Ibelin” will be one of the talking points of the French-Nordic Producers’ Conversation.

	Seven of the Nordic’s top literary agencies will also be on-site for the Books in Haugesund session.

	Full list of Nordic Co-production Market Lineup:

title: DGA and IATSE Push Rob Bonta to Allow Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger With Conditions
description: The Directors Guild of America and IATSE are urging California Attorney General Rob Bonta to settle his antitrust lawsuit with Paramount, arguing th
body:
The Directors Guild of America and IATSE are urging California Attorney General Rob Bonta to settle his antitrust lawsuit with Paramount, arguing that prolonged uncertainty over the Warner Bros. Discovery merger is bad for the industry.

	The two unions wrote a letter to Bonta and Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison on Wednesday, urging the two sides to come to an agreement that would include conditions to address concerns over harms to competition.
	

	“While we have been consistent in our view that mergers, such as this one, historically offer few benefits to workers, we are also particularly concerned about the negative impact a delay in the decision regarding the proposed merger will have on our members and the industry at large,” the two unions wrote.


	The letter puts the two unions at odds with the Writers Guild of America, which filed its own antitrust suit to try to block the merger. The antitrust case has created other divisions within the industry, as both Regal Cinemas and AMC Theatres have endorsed the merger, while the theater trade group — Cinema United — adamantly opposes it.

	Bonta led a coalition of 12 states to sue to block the merger in July, arguing that the deal creates illegal consolidation in the basic cable and theatrical distribution markets. Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin issued a temporary retraining order to pause the deal, and last week set a March 2 trial date, four months later than Paramount’s preferred schedule.

	Ellison has been working to rally support for the deal within the industry,  while also trying to bring pressure on Bonta to come to the negotiating table. Bonta has repeatedly said that he is not interested in “behavioral” remedies — such as a pledge to release 30 movies a year with a 45-day window — but is focused on a structural solution, which Paramount has thus far been unwilling to entertain.
	

	The letter was signed by Russell Hollander, national executive director of the DGA, and by Matthew Loeb, the international president of IATSE. The letter argues that the March 2 trial date is “damaging” to an “already struggling industry.”

	“As our members struggle to find employment, the uncertainty surrounding the proposed merger is only making matters worse,” the letter states. “We are aware of productions that have been put on hold or canceled altogether, leading to further reductions in available work for our members and other industry workers.”

	The letter urges the two sides to agree on conditions, many of which Paramount has already agreed to, such as the maintenance of the two studios as separate entities that will each produce at least 15 films a year. The unions also suggest that Paramount commit to continue licensing content from outside production companies at the same rate as before the merger.

	If the states and Paramount cannot reach a deal, the unions urge them both to agree to an earlier trial date. However, while Paramount has been eager for an accelerated timeline, the states asked the judge for time to depose Paramount executives and obtain documents in order to bolster its case.

            Jenna Jameson is taking another stab at marriage ... because the ex-porn star has tied the knot with her partner Milagros Ocampo, TMZ has learned.

            Let's hope things go better for Jenna on the second go around. Congrats Jenna and Milagros!!!

title: Lauren Boebert's Son Accepts Plea Deal in Child Abuse Case
description:
Lauren Boebert's Son Tyler
                          Accepts Plea Deal in Child Abuse Case
body:
Lauren Boebert's Son Tyler
                          Accepts Plea Deal in Child Abuse Case
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 13, 2026
                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Lauren Boebert’s son Tyler Boebert accepted a plea deal from prosecutors in his child abuse case could end up with him serving some jail time ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court docs obtained by TMZ, the Weld County District Attorney’s Office offered a deal in which Tyler would plead guilty to the charges of child abuse/negligence without injury.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The District Attorney said it suggested the court sentence Tyler to a cap of 30 days in jail and 12-month supervised probation.
      
    
            The prosecutors also want him to complete a parenting program.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Tyler was charged with child abuse/negligence without injury after authorities say his baby was found wandering around the neighborhood in July 2025.
      
    
            Months later, prosecutors claimed there was a second incident that occurred one month before the July 2025 incident. The docs state the baby was unattended and “wandering around” in just a diaper, while under Tyler’s care before a neighbor spotted the kid.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Before the news of the second alleged incident, Rep. Boebert defended her son publicly, saying “Tyler has been doing a great job getting his life on track as a father and citizen over the past year."
      
    
            Rep. Boebert added, “Unfortunately, this event stems from a miscommunication on monitoring my young grandson that recently led to him getting out of our house.”
      
    
            As TMZ first reported, Tyler was arrested this weekend on charges of child sexual exploitation. According to law enforcement, the charges stem from a video he filmed when he was 18 with his then-girlfriend, who was weeks away from turning 18. She apparently contacted police after the tape leaked to third parties.
